questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Rational Functions With Repeated Factors of Degree Two That Require Factoring
questions.worked_solution:
Let's first factor the denominator of the integrand:

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}-2x-5}{{x}^{3}-5{x}^{2}}=\frac{{x}^{2}-2x-5}{{x}^{2}(x-5)}
$$

We must convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}-2x-5}{{x}^{2}(x-5)}=\frac{A}{x}+\frac{B}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{C}{(x-5)}.
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by ${x}^{2}(x-5)$ and get

$$
{x}^{2}-2x-5=A(x)(x-5)+B(x-5)+C{x}^{2}.
$$

Plugging in $x=5,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $B$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}({5}^{2})-2(5)-5 & =A(5)(5-5)+B(5-5)+C(5)^{2} \\ 10 & =C(25) \\ C & =\frac{10}{25} \\ C & =\frac{2}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, plugging in $x=0,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $C$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(0)^{2}-2(0)-5 & =A(0)(0-5)+B(0-5)+C(0)^{2} \\ -5 & =B(-5) \\ B & =\frac{-5}{-5} \\ B & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, plugging in $x=1$ and substituting the known values of $B$ and $C,$ we can solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}({1}^{2})-2(1)-5 & =A(1)(1-5)+B(1-5)+C(1)^{2} \\ -6 & =-4A-4B+C \\ -6 & =-4A-4(1)+(\frac{2}{5}) \\ 4A & =6-4+\frac{2}{5} \\ 4A & =\frac{10+2}{5} \\ A & =\frac{12}{20} \\ A & =\frac{3}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integrand as the partial sum

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}-2x-5}{{x}^{2}(x-5)}=\frac{3}{5x}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{2}{5(x-5)}.
$$

Finally, we integrate this expression term by term to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}-2x-5}{{x}^{2}(x-5)}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{3}{5x}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{2}{5(x-5)})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\int \frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+\frac{2}{5}\int \frac{1}{x-5}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|-\frac{1}{x}+\frac{2}{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-5|+K,\end{aligned}
$$

where $K$ is an integral constant.

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating Rational Functions With a Repeated Factor and Another Factor
questions.worked_solution:
First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{(x-2)(x-3)^{2}}=\frac{A}{x-2}+\frac{B}{x-3}+\frac{C}{(x-3)^{2}}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,$ $B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(x-2)(x-3)^{2}$ and get

$$
{x}^{2}=A(x-3)^{2}+B(x-3)(x-2)+C(x-2).
$$

Plugging in $x=3,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $B$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(3)^{2} & =A(3-3)^{2}+B(3-3)(3-2)+C(3-2) \\ 9 & =C \\ C & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=2,$  we can eliminate  $B$ and $C$ and solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(2)^{2} & =A(2-3)^{2}+B(2-3)(2-2)+C(2-2) \\ 4 & =A \\ A & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known values of $A$ and $C,$ we can solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(0)^{2} & =A(0-3)^{2}+B(0-3)(0-2)+C(0-2) \\ 0 & =9A+6B-2C \\ 0 & =9(4)+6B-2(9) \\ 0 & =18+6B \\ -6B & =18 \\ B & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{(x-2)(x-3)^{2}}=\frac{4}{x-2}-\frac{3}{x-3}+\frac{9}{(x-3)^{2}}.
$$

Finally, we integrate this expression term by term, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}}{(x-2)(x-3)^{2}}\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{4}{x-2}-\frac{3}{x-3}+\frac{9}{(x-3)^{2}})\text{d}x \\  & =4\int \frac{1}{x-2}\,\text{d}x-3\int \frac{1}{x-3}\,\text{d}x+9\int \frac{1}{(x-3)^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =4\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|-3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-3|-\frac{9}{x-3}+K,\end{aligned}
$$

where $K$ is an integral constant.

questions.worked_solution:
First, we convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}-9x+21}{(x-4)^{2}(3-x)}=\frac{A}{(x-4)}+\frac{B}{(x-4)^{2}}+\frac{C}{(3-x)}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,$ $B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(x-4)^{2}(3-x)$ and get

$$
{x}^{2}-9x+21=A(x-4)(3-x)+B(3-x)+C(x-4)^{2}.
$$

Plugging in $x=4,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $C$ and solve for $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{4}^{2}-9(4)+21 & =A(4-4)(3-4)+B(3-4)+C(4-4)^{2} \\ 16-36+21 & =B(-1) \\ 1 & =-B \\ B & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=3,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $B$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{2}-9(3)+21 & =A(3-4)(3-3)+B(3-3)+C(3-4)^{2} \\ 9-27+21 & =C{(-1)}^{2} \\ C & =\frac{3}{1} \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known values of $B$ and $C,$ we can solve for $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{0}^{2}-9(0)+21 & =A(0-4)(3-0)+B(3-0)+C(0-4)^{2} \\ 21 & =-12A+3B+16C \\ 21 & =-12A+3(-1)+16(3) \\ 21 & =-12A+45 \\ 12A & =45-21 \\ A & =\frac{24}{12} \\ A & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}-9x+21}{(x-4)^{2}(3-x)}=\frac{2}{(x-4)}-\frac{1}{(x-4)^{2}}+\frac{3}{(3-x)}.
$$

Finally, we integrate this expression term by term, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{5}^{6}\frac{{x}^{2}-9x+21}{(x-4)^{2}(3-x)}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{5}^{6}(\frac{2}{(x-4)}-\frac{1}{(x-4)^{2}}+\frac{3}{(3-x)})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{\int }_{5}^{6}\frac{1}{x-4}\,\text{d}x-{\int }_{5}^{6}\frac{1}{(x-4)^{2}}\,\text{d}x+3{\int }_{5}^{6}\frac{1}{3-x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-4|{|}_{5}^{6}+\frac{1}{x-4}{|}_{5}^{6}-3\operatorname{ln}⁡|3-x|{|}_{5}^{6} \\  & =2(\operatorname{ln}⁡|6-4|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|5-4|)+(\frac{1}{6-4}-\frac{1}{5-4})-3(\operatorname{ln}⁡|3-6|-\operatorname{ln}⁡|3-5|) \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡2-\frac{1}{2}-3\operatorname{ln}⁡3+3\operatorname{ln}⁡2 \\  & =5\operatorname{ln}⁡2-3\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Functions With a Repeated Factor of Degree Higher Than Two
questions.worked_solution:
First, we must convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}+4x}{(x+2)^{3}}=\frac{A}{x+2}+\frac{B}{(x+2)^{2}}+\frac{C}{(x+2)^{3}}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(x+2)^{3}$ and get

$$
{x}^{2}+4x=A(x+2)^{2}+B(x+2)+C.
$$

Plugging in $x=-2,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $B$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-2)^{2}+4(-2) & =A(-2+2)^{2}+B(-2+2)+C \\ -4 & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Now, plugging in $x=0$ and substituting the known value of $C,$ we get an equation relating $A$ and $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(0)^{2}+4(0) & =A(0+2)^{2}+B(0+2)+C \\ 0 & =4A+2B-4 \\ 2A+B & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, plugging in $x=-1$ and substituting the known value of $C,$ we get an equation relating $A$ and $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)^{2}+4(-1) & =A(-1+2)^{2}+B(-1+2)+C \\ -3 & =A+B-4 \\ A+B & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the equations $2A+B=2$ and $A+B=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =2-1 \\ A & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting back into $A+B=1,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1+B & =1 \\ B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integrand as the partial sum

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}+4x}{(x+2)^{3}}=\frac{1}{x+2}-\frac{4}{(x+2)^{3}}.
$$

Finally, we integrate this expression term by term to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}+4x}{(x+2)^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{x+2}-\frac{4}{(x+2)^{3}})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x+2}\,\text{d}x-\int \frac{4}{(x+2)^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x+2|+\frac{2}{(x+2)^{2}}+K,\end{aligned}
$$

where $K$ is an integral constant.

questions.knowledge_point: Integrating a Rational Functions With a Repeated Factor of Degree Higher Than Two
questions.worked_solution:
First, we must convert the integrand into a sum of partial fractions:

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}-3x+3}{(x-2)^{3}}=\frac{A}{x-2}+\frac{B}{(x-2)^{2}}+\frac{C}{(x-2)^{3}}
$$

To determine the coefficients $A,B,$ and $C,$ we first multiply both sides of the above equation by $(x-2)^{3}$ and get

$$
{x}^{2}-3x+3=A(x-2)^{2}+B(x-2)+C.
$$

Plugging in $x=2,$ we can eliminate $A$ and $B$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(2)^{2}-3(2)+3 & =A(2-2)^{2}+B(2-2)+C \\ 1 & =C\end{aligned}
$$

Now, plugging in $x=1$ and substituting the known value of $C,$ we get an equation relating $A$ and $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(1)^{2}-3(1)+3 & =A(1-2)^{2}+B(1-2)+C \\ 1 & =A-B+1 \\ A-B & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly, plugging in $x=3$ and substituting the known value of $C,$ we get an equation relating $A$ and $B:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(3)^{2}-3(3)+3 & =A(3-2)^{2}+B(3-2)+C \\ 3 & =A+B+1 \\ A+B & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Adding the equations $A-B=0$ and $A+B=2,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2A & =0+2 \\ 2A & =2 \\ A & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

 
and substituting back into $A-B=0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}1-B & =0 \\ B & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integrand as the partial sum

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}-3x+3}{(x-2)^{3}}=\frac{1}{x-2}+\frac{1}{(x-2)^{2}}+\frac{1}{(x-2)^{3}}.
$$

Finally, we integrate this expression term by term to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{2}-3x+3}{(x-2)^{3}}\,\text{d}x & =\int (\frac{1}{x-2}+\frac{1}{(x-2)^{2}}+\frac{1}{(x-2)^{3}})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{x-2}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{(x-2)^{2}}\,\text{d}x+\int \frac{1}{(x-2)^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡|x-2|-\frac{1}{x-2}-\frac{1}{2(x-2)^{2}}+K,\end{aligned}
$$

where $K$ is an integral constant.
